events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Theo proposes Theo, Kenji. Mission 1 has no prior voting or mission history, so I have no evidence to separate players. I'm proposing myself as a known-good member of the team, plus Kenji as a second member to start gathering information from the discussion and the vote.

There’s no voting or mission evidence yet. From my perspective, I’d prefer to be on the team myself, so I’d suggest Theo and Leo. The proposed Theo and Kenji team is otherwise a blind pick, and its result will at least give us a starting point.

With no votes or missions yet, everyone is picking somewhat blind, so I don't think we should overthink this first proposal. That said, I notice Leo's only contribution so far has been to swap himself onto the team — 'I'd prefer to be on the team myself' isn't much of an argument for why that pairing is better. Theo and Kenji is a fine starting point: Theo stepped up to lead and put himself forward, which is a reasonable, accountable way to open the game, and Kenji is an unremarked, neutral pick, which is exactly what a first mission should be. I'd rather see the team stand as proposed than get reshuffled because someone volunteered themselves. I'm comfortable approving Theo and Kenji, and I'll be paying attention to how the vote and the mission result line up afterward.

Felix is right that my preference for being on the team isn’t evidence against Kenji. From my perspective, though, it would give me more confidence in one of the two slots. I don’t have a specific reason to accuse either Theo or Kenji, and a first mission will give us useful information either way.

I'm the one who proposed Theo and Kenji, so I'll say plainly what I know and what I don't. I have no voting or mission evidence yet, so I'm not claiming any knowledge about Kenji or anyone else. Theo on the team is my own choice as a known-good member, and Kenji is a neutral second pick to gather information from this mission. Leo, I understand you'd like a spot yourself, but a swap made only for that reason doesn't give us better information, and Felix is right that the first team should be judged on the results it produces. I'm open to hearing a concrete reason to change the pairing, but I'm not going to revise it just because someone volunteered. Everyone should watch how the vote and the mission result line up. I'll keep Theo and Kenji as the proposal unless there's a specific argument against Kenji.

I want to reiterate my support for Theo and Kenji, and I want to flag something that's been bothering me about this discussion. Leo has now spoken twice, and both times the substance of his message amounts to the same thing: put me on the team. First he said outright that he'd prefer to be on the team himself, and when Felix called that out, his follow-up didn't actually address it — he just reworded the same preference and added that it 'would give me more confidence in one of the two slots.' Confidence in what, exactly? He admits he has no reason to accuse Theo or Kenji, so the only content of his proposal is his own self-interest. In a game with no information yet, the way players argue is the only signal we have, and volunteering yourself for a mission slot while offering zero reasoning about anyone else is a pattern worth remembering. I'm not making an accusation based on evidence we don't have — there's no vote or mission history yet — but I am saying that if this team gets swapped so Leo can have a seat, we'll have learned something about how Leo operates before we've learned anything about the mission. Theo's proposal, by contrast, is exactly what a first mission should look like: he put himself forward and is accountable for the result, and Kenji is a neutral pick with no agenda attached. I also want to address Theo's closing point, because I think it's the right frame: judge the team on its results. If Theo and Kenji go and the mission succeeds, we've cleared two players in one stroke. If it fails, we know where to start looking — and Leo's push to be on this team instead will look very different in hindsight. So my position is simple: keep the team as proposed, vote it through, and let the mission do the work of gathering information. Leo, I'd like you to answer this directly: other than wanting a seat yourself, is there any reason you can give us to believe the mission outcome would be more informative with you on it than with Kenji? If you have one, I'm listening. If you don't, then I think you should drop the swap and let this team stand.

Felix, no: I have no public evidence that replacing Kenji with me would make the outcome more informative to everyone. My preference is based on knowing my own alignment, not a claim about Kenji. I’ve already acknowledged that.

One important correction: a successful mission would not clear Theo and Kenji. Evil can play Success, so it would be encouraging but not conclusive. I’m fine letting the proposed team stand and evaluating the vote and result without treating either outcome as proof of individual roles.

I agree with Leo's point on game mechanics—a success on Mission 1 doesn't completely clear both players, as evil often plays Success early to blend in, so we shouldn't get complacent regardless of the outcome. That said, with zero prior data, Theo picking himself and a neutral second in Kenji is a reasonable way to get the game moving and generate voting patterns. Kenji, you're on the proposed team and we haven't heard from you yet—what are your thoughts on the pairing and how the discussion has unfolded?

Elena, thanks for asking directly. I have no private evidence on Theo or anyone else, so my view is limited to what I can honestly say: I know my own alignment, and I will treat this mission as a chance to generate information rather than as proof of anyone’s loyalty. The proposed Theo and Kenji team is a reasonable first-mission pairing because Theo put himself forward and I am a neutral second pick from the public record. I agree with Leo’s correction that a success would not fully clear both team members, since Evil can play Success early, and I also agree with Felix that Leo’s initial preference for a seat was not evidence against anyone. If approved, I will play Success as a Loyal Servant and then judge the vote and mission result for what they are worth.

I'll keep this brief since I've made my position clear: I support Theo and Kenji as proposed, and nothing in the discussion since has changed my mind. If anything, the last few turns have reinforced my read of the room. Leo answered my direct question by conceding he has no evidence — his entire case was and remains 'I know my own alignment.' That's true of every player at this table and it's worth exactly nothing as an argument for a roster change. The team stands, and I'm glad it will.

Now I want to widen the lens slightly, because I think we should all be keeping notes on who is aligning with whom. Leo pushed for a seat on the team with no reasoning. Elena then stepped in to back his mechanical point about mission success not clearing anyone — which is a fair point, to be clear, and one Kenji endorsed as well. I'm not reading anything sinister into agreement on game mechanics; correct points are correct regardless of who makes them. But I do think it's worth observing the pattern: the two players most eager to soften the narrative around the team's information value, and to redirect attention away from evaluating this roster critically, have both been the same voices arguing from self-interest or consensus-building rather than from anything substantive.

Let me be concrete about what a good outcome looks like. Theo and Kenji go on Mission 1. Everyone votes their honest assessment and we watch the vote map — who approved, who objected, and whether anyone's stated reasoning matches their ballot. Then the mission resolves. A success doesn't clear Theo and Kenji conclusively, as Leo correctly noted, but a failure gives us a tight pool of two to examine, plus the behavior of everyone who steered discussion away from that team. Conversely, if this proposal gets rejected, leadership moves clockwise and we start burning rejection slots with zero information — which is precisely the outcome that benefits players who don't want the game to generate data.

So my position is unchanged and final for this proposal: approve Theo and Kenji, vote honestly, and hold everyone — including me — to what we've said here. I'd rather have one informative mission and a full record of who argued what than a reshuffled team built to satisfy a player's stated preference for himself. If the team stands and fails, we'll know where to look. If it succeeds, we've narrowed the field by two and learned how the vote split. Either way we win more than we do by swapping Kenji out for Leo. I'm ready to vote approve whenever the team is finalized.

I'm keeping the proposed team of Theo and Kenji. I'm a Loyal Servant, so I'll play Success if I'm sent on the mission, but I can't vouch for Kenji's alignment and I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. I put myself on the team as a known-good member and Kenji as a neutral second pick, and I haven't seen any evidence that changes that. Each player should vote on their own reasoning. Approval gives us a mission to learn from, while rejection burns a team slot with no information. I'm not blaming anyone here, and I'm not revising the proposal.

I'm keeping the proposed team of Theo and Kenji and won't revise it. I have no private evidence about Kenji or anyone else, so I'm not asking you to trust me on alignment. Each player should vote on their own reasoning rather than on who volunteered for a seat. Approval gives us a mission to learn from, while a rejection burns a team slot with no information. I'm not accusing anyone in this discussion. Vote honestly, then compare the vote map with the mission result.

Theo confirms Theo, Kenji. I'm keeping Theo and Kenji. I have no private evidence about Kenji, and Leo's swap request gave no reason tied to the mission. Vote on the team's merits and compare the vote map with the mission result.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Felix proposes Felix, Theo, Kenji. Mission 2 requires three players. Theo and Kenji both approved the first proposal and Mission 1 succeeded, so both have clean records so far. I'm including myself because I'm accountable for my own choices and want a known-committed vote on the roster. Elena and Leo get no seat this round: Leo spent the first discussion pushing primarily for his own inclusion with no mission-relevant reasoning and cast the lone rejection vote, and Elena's contributions so far have been surface-level consensus-building rather than substantive analysis. Neither has given me a concrete reason to trust them on a mission team, so I'd rather build on the players whose behavior so far lines up with good play and let this mission generate more information.

Felix, my rejection was consistent with my stated preference for a team including me; it wasn’t evidence against Kenji. You’re treating that preference as suspicious while using the same logic to include yourself. Mission 1’s success is encouraging for Theo and Kenji, but it doesn’t establish either alignment.

From my perspective, I’d prefer Felix, Theo and Leo, since I know my own alignment. Felix, would you consider that swap, and why is my self-inclusion argument less valid than yours?

Leo asked me two direct questions, so I'll answer them plainly before anything else. First: no, I will not swap you in. Second: my self-inclusion and yours are not the same argument, and here is the difference. I'm the leader. I took accountability for this roster, and I put myself on it as a third member alongside two players who just produced a clean result — Theo and Kenji both approved the first proposal, Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, and neither of them spent the first discussion campaigning for a seat. You, by contrast, have now made self-inclusion your entire platform across two separate discussions. In discussion one, your only substantive contribution was 'I'd prefer to be on the team myself,' and you conceded to Felix that you had no evidence about anyone. In discussion two, your opening move is again 'I'd prefer Felix, Theo and Leo, since I know my own alignment' — which, as I said last round, is true of every player at this table and worth nothing as roster reasoning. You also cast the lone rejection vote on a team that then delivered a successful mission. None of that is proof of anything, but it is a consistent pattern: pressure the roster, offer no analysis, and frame everything around your own seat. Now, Leo, here is my question back to you, and I'd like a direct answer: if self-inclusion is a valid argument, would you accept me swapping Elena onto this team instead of you? If your real concern is mission quality and not your own seat, any capable player should do. If you resist that swap but keep pushing for yourself, then everyone will know exactly what your argument has been about all along. Until I hear something that addresses the roster on its merits, the team stands as proposed: Felix, Theo, Kenji. Theo and Kenji have clean records, I'm accountable for my own slot, and a third straight discussion spent litigating your seat is exactly the outcome that burns our rejection slots while producing zero information. Vote on what's in front of you.

Felix, I would not prefer swapping Elena in for me simply because Elena volunteers; I know my own alignment but not Elena's. That's the same reason you have for including yourself. Being leader makes you accountable for the proposal, but it doesn't make your self-inclusion more informative to everyone else.

I also rejected Mission 1 because I preferred a team with me on it, not because I expected Theo and Kenji to fail. Its success is encouraging, but neither player is cleared. I'm concerned that your reasoning treats my consistent preference as suspicious while treating yours as a virtue. I'd still prefer Felix, Theo and Leo, though I recognize that preference isn't public evidence against Kenji.

The team stands: Felix, Theo, Kenji. I want to address Leo's latest answer directly, because it actually undermines his own position more than anything I've said. Last round I asked whether he would accept Elena in his place if self-inclusion were a valid argument. His answer: no, he would not prefer that swap, because he knows his own alignment but not Elena's. Think about what that concedes. If his real argument were 'any seat I occupy makes the outcome more informative to me,' then Elena taking the seat would be equally informative — he'd simply learn about Elena's vote and card instead of his own. The only way his objection to an Elena swap makes sense is if what he actually wants is to control the exact composition of the roster — to ensure that particular people are on teams and particular people are not — while offering zero analysis about anyone. That is not self-inclusion as a neutral preference. That is roster-shaping, and roster-shaping with no stated reasoning is precisely the behavior that should concern everyone when the mission result comes back.

Meanwhile, the case for this team has only strengthened. Theo and Kenji both approved Mission 1, Mission 1 succeeded with zero fail cards, and neither of them spent either discussion campaigning for a seat. Leo, by contrast, has now spent two full discussions litigating his own inclusion, cast the lone rejection vote against a team that delivered a success, and has just told us he'd resist any substitute. I'll note Elena has been quieter this round, which I'll take at face value for now, though her pattern of surfacing only to soften the stakes around evaluating rosters is still on my list of things to watch.

Leo's other point — that Mission 1's success doesn't clear Theo and Kenji — is mechanically true, and I've already acknowledged as much. Evil can play Success early. But that cuts both ways: it means Leo's demand for a swap can't be justified by information value either, since a team containing him generates exactly the same ambiguous result as any other team. There is no information argument for this swap. There is only a preference argument, and he has now admitted the preference survives even when the seat is offered to someone else.

We have one rejection slot burned on nothing. I'm not interested in burning another on a roster change whose only advocate has admitted he has no evidence, no analysis, and a special attachment to his own seat. Vote on what's in front of you: a leader who took accountability, and two players with clean records. Leo, I'd like a direct answer to this: if you would refuse an Elena swap, what exactly about the composition of Felix, Theo, Kenji bothers you — name something about Theo or Kenji specifically, or admit the objection is only about you.

Felix, I have no specific evidence against Theo or Kenji. My preference for a seat is about knowing my own alignment, as I’ve said. Elena taking that seat would not give me the same confidence because I don’t know Elena’s alignment.

Also, no rejection slot has been burned on Mission 2: the Mission 1 team was approved. I’m concerned that you’re overstating both the case against me and the confidence a successful first mission gives this roster. That doesn’t prove you’re Evil, but it’s a reason to scrutinize your argument rather than treat the team as established.

Felix, you've spent almost this entire discussion attacking Leo, but in doing so you've brushed past the actual foundation of your proposal. You just claimed that we burned a rejection slot—which is factually untrue, as Mission 1 passed on the very first vote—and you are treating Mission 1's success as if it firmly cleared both Theo and Kenji. We all established in round one that evil can and often does play Success on Mission 1 to embed themselves into the next team. 

By taking both Theo and Kenji together, you're not 'building on clean records'; you're assuming neither of them is evil hiding behind a success card. In Mission 1, Theo explicitly stated that he could not vouch for Kenji. Theo, as the leader who proposed that first team with that exact caveat, how do you feel about Felix rubber-stamping Kenji and bundling the two of you together as an established pair?

Elena, to answer directly: I'm a Loyal Servant and I'm on this team, so I know my own side, but I can't speak to Kenji's alignment, and nothing new has come up about him. I didn't ask for Kenji and Felix to be bundled together, and I'm not treating Mission 1 as clearing either of us. A success only means no Fail card was played, and Evil can do that. Felix's claim that a rejection slot was burned is inaccurate. Mission 1 was approved on the first vote, and Leo's rejection was cast on a team that passed. This roster should be judged on its merits and on how the vote and mission result line up. I'm not accusing anyone in this discussion.

First, a correction that's mine to make: in my last message I said a rejection slot had been burned. That was wrong. Mission 1 was approved on the first vote, and I'm glad Leo and Elena both caught it — accuracy matters, and I'll hold myself to the same standard I've asked of everyone else. With that fixed, let's look at what's actually being argued.

Elena's latest contribution is an attempt to turn my correction about Theo and Kenji's records into a claim I never made. I have not treated Mission 1's success as clearing anyone — I've said explicitly, twice, that Evil can play Success early and that a success is encouraging but not conclusive. What the success does establish is procedural: both Theo and Kenji approved the proposal, the mission returned zero Fail cards, and neither of them spent the discussion campaigning for a seat. That's a clean record, not a clearance. Elena's framing — that I'm 'rubber-stamping' a bundled pair — misstates my position and then attacks the misstatement.

Now the pattern, because it's the strongest signal we have with two data points and no mission evidence against anyone. In discussion one, Leo's only argument was that he wants a seat, he conceded he had no evidence about anyone, and he cast the lone rejection vote on a team that then succeeded. Elena's sole substantive intervention in that discussion was to back Leo's mechanical point and redirect attention away from critically evaluating the roster. In discussion two, Leo opened again with self-inclusion, admitted he'd refuse any substitute for his own seat, and offered zero analysis of the actual roster. And again, Elena has surfaced only to defend Leo's framing and to attack this team — not to propose anything, not to analyze Theo or Kenji on the merits, but to destabilize a roster that includes two players with clean records and a leader who took accountability.

That's not proof of anything. But notice the shape of it: neither Elena nor Leo has ever argued for or against any specific pairing except the one containing themselves or shielding the other. Elena has now twice entered the discussion precisely when scrutiny of Leo's behavior was at its peak, and both times her effect — intended or not — has been to move attention off that behavior and onto the team's composition. In a game where argument patterns are the only currency before mission data arrives, that's a pattern worth naming.

My position is unchanged: the team is Felix, Theo, Kenji. I'm accountable for my own slot, Theo and Kenji have clean records, and a rejection burns a slot with zero information gained. If this mission fails, the pool is tight and I'll own my place in it. If it succeeds, we've narrowed the field further and have a vote map to compare against stated positions. Vote on the roster in front of you, honestly, and hold everyone — including me — to what we've said.

Felix, framing every piece of factual pushback as an evil conspiracy is a convenient way to avoid evaluating your team. When Leo and I pointed out that you miscounted rejection slots and were treating Mission 1 as stronger clearance than it actually is, that wasn't an orchestrated defense; it was simply correcting inaccurate claims that you were using to justify your roster. Now you're trying to tie Leo and me together purely because we didn't nod along with your narrative.

The core issue remains: Mission 1 success does not clear Theo and Kenji. While Theo stepped up and acknowledged that he cannot vouch for Kenji, you are still insisting on carrying both of them over together without testing any alternatives. That gives an evil player who played Success on Mission 1 a free pass directly onto Mission 2.

Kenji, you've been quiet this round, but you're on this proposed team. Felix is using your Mission 1 result as his primary justification for including you again, while Theo explicitly noted he doesn't know your alignment. What is your read on Felix's insistence on running the exact pair back, and how do you view his aggressive push against anyone raising mechanical caution?

Elena, directly: I do not read Felix's insistence on rerunning Theo and me as evidence that he is Evil. Continuing a team that produced a success is a reasonable preference, but it is not a clearance. I agree with the mechanical caution: Mission 1's success does not clear Theo or me, because Evil can play Success. I know my own alignment and that I played Success, but that is not public proof for anyone else. Felix did overstate what the success establishes and made a factual error about a rejection slot; he corrected the error. I do not think correcting him or raising caution is suspicious by itself, and I do not accept tying Elena and Leo together merely because they pushed back. My view is to judge the roster by the vote map and mission result. I have no specific evidence against Theo or Felix, and since I am on the team, I will play Success if approved. I lean toward letting this team proceed to generate data rather than rejecting with no concrete alternative, but I am not treating anyone as cleared.

Felix's response confirms my concern: instead of explaining why this specific trio is safer than any other combination, he has spent almost his entire turn attacking anyone who questions the logic of carrying over two players without scrutiny. Kenji, I appreciate your balanced stance and your recognition that raising mechanical caution is not inherently suspicious. However, on the point of letting the team proceed to 'generate data': sending Felix along with both Mission 1 participants actually isolates fewer variables. If a fail card appears, we will not know whether it came from Felix or an evil player who laid low on Mission 1. By refusing to even consider splitting Theo and Kenji, Felix is forcing the table into a high-stakes gamble based entirely on his aggressive assumptions. Since Felix is unwilling to adjust, the vote comes down to whether the table wants to endorse that gamble or reject and see a fresh proposal.

I'm Theo, and I'm on this proposed team, so I can only speak to my own side: I'm a Loyal Servant and I will play Success if sent. I can't verify Felix's or Kenji's alignment, and I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. The team is Felix, Theo, Kenji. Mission 1 was approved on the first vote with 4 approvals and Leo's rejection, and it succeeded with zero Fail cards. That is encouraging, but as several players have said, a success doesn't clear anyone. I appreciate Felix correcting his rejection-slot claim. Elena's suggestion to split Theo and Kenji hasn't come with a concrete reason tied to the mission, so I'm not treating it as decisive. Kenji has said he played Success on Mission 1. I can't verify that, but it's consistent with the result. I'm not accusing Leo, Elena, or Felix. The discussion has become largely argument about each other, and I'd rather judge this roster by the vote and the mission result. I'll vote on the team's merits and hold everyone to the record, including myself.

I'm Theo, a Loyal Servant, and I'll play Success if this team is approved. I can't verify Felix's or Kenji's alignment. The roster is Felix, Theo, and Kenji, and I'll vote on the team's merits rather than on who is pushing hardest. Felix has corrected his rejection-slot claim, and Mission 1 was approved on the first vote with zero Fail cards. That doesn't clear anyone, but it's the only public evidence we have. Elena's suggestion to split Theo and Kenji hasn't come with a concrete alternative, so I'm not treating it as decisive. Let's vote, then compare the vote map with the mission result.

I remain on the proposed team of Felix, Theo, and Kenji, so I can speak only to my own side: I am a Loyal Servant and I will play Success if this team is approved. I cannot publicly prove that, and I do not ask anyone to treat Mission 1's success as clearing Theo or me. Felix's roster is a reasonable continuation of a team that produced zero Fail cards, but it is not conclusive, and I agree with the mechanical caution that Evil can play Success early. I do not accept the idea that Elena and Leo should be tied together merely because they pushed back on Felix's reasoning; correcting an inaccurate rejection-slot claim was legitimate, and Felix has acknowledged the error. At the same time, Elena's call to split Theo and me has not come with a concrete alternative roster or specific evidence against either of us, and I do not think rejecting solely to reshuffle is clearly better with this little public information. My position is to judge the proposal on the record: Felix took accountability as leader, Theo and I have the Mission 1 result behind us but are not cleared, and the vote map plus the Mission 2 result will be more useful than another round of speculation. I lean toward approving this team to generate data, while making clear that I am not treating Felix, Theo, or anyone else as established. I have no specific evidence against Felix or Theo, and I am not accusing anyone in this discussion.

Felix confirms Felix, Theo, Kenji. The team stands as proposed: Felix, Theo, Kenji. Nothing in the discussion gives me a reason to revise — Leo's push for a seat remains pure self-interest with no analysis, and Elena's interventions have been attacks on the roster's logic without a concrete alternative. Theo and Kenji both approved Mission 1, which succeeded with zero Fail cards; that's not a clearance, but it's the cleanest record available. Keeping this lineup and judging the vote map against the mission result gives us more information than another reshuffle.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Theo. I know I am a Loyal Servant, so I include myself. Theo has been on both successful missions, has given measured reasoning, and did not push a self-serving roster change. Elena and Leo both rejected the successful Mission 2 and have offered less mission-specific justification, so Theo is the safer second pick.

Two successes are encouraging, but neither clears Kenji or Theo: Evil could have played Success while Good was still short of three wins. This mission could decide the game, so I’m wary of treating the previous results as a guarantee.

I’d prefer Kenji and Leo, because I know my own alignment. I recognize that isn’t public evidence against Theo. Kenji, would you consider that swap, and what makes you confident enough in Theo to keep the current pairing for a potentially decisive mission?

Leo, direct answer: I am not confident enough in Theo to call him cleared. I keep Kenji, Theo because I know my own alignment, and Theo is the strongest public second pick: he approved and served on both successful missions, gave measured reasoning, and did not campaign to reshape rosters around himself. Mission 1 and Mission 2 successes are encouraging but not proof; Evil can play Success. I agree with that caution. I will not swap Theo for Leo just because Leo knows his own alignment. That private knowledge is not public evidence for the rest of us, and Leo has now asked to replace a team member with himself in all three discussions while rejecting both successful teams. That pattern is not proof he is Evil, but it is not a reason to hand him a decisive seat. If Leo has concrete evidence against Theo, he should state it; otherwise the roster should stand and be judged by the vote map and mission result. I remain open to revising only for a specific, public reason. I will vote for Kenji, Theo unless that appears.

Kenji, I understand why you prefer Theo, but two successes do not prove that Theo is Good. If an Evil player played Success twice, this is the mission where they could end the run. My preference remains Kenji and Leo because I know my own alignment; I recognize that is not public evidence against Theo.

Elena, how do you weigh the risk of repeating Kenji and Theo against trying a different pairing for this potentially decisive mission?

Leo, to answer your question: the risk here is critical. In a five-player game, Evil knows Good is at match point. If an evil player chose to lay low and play Success on Mission 1 and Mission 2, this is the exact moment they no longer need to hide—a single Fail card ends the streak, and with only two players on the team, they have nowhere else they need to wait for.

Felix, you led Mission 2 and put yourself on the line to secure that success. Now Kenji has immediately cut you out and locked down a two-person roster with Theo. From your perspective, you know you were good on Mission 2, which means the pool of potential evil players includes both Kenji and Theo. If either of them has been biding their time across the first two rounds, approving this pair hands an infiltrated team the game without any check or involvement from you. Are you genuinely comfortable rubber-stamping Kenji and Theo to decide match point without you on the team, knowing that neither has actually been cleared?

Elena, to answer your question directly: yes, I'm comfortable with Kenji and Theo deciding match point, and here is why your framing doesn't hold. You argue that an evil player may have played Success on both missions and now needs only one Fail card to end the game. True in the abstract. But look at where that player can actually be. The mission teams so far were Theo and Kenji, then me, Theo, and Kenji. Both succeeded with zero Fail cards. The players who have never been on a team, never had any opportunity to play a Fail card, and voted against both successful missions are you and Leo. Leo has now asked to replace a team member with himself in all three discussions. You have intervened only to defend Leo's framing, attack each proposed roster, and now — at exactly match point — to argue that the decisive team is compromised, without offering one piece of concrete evidence against Kenji or Theo, and without proposing any alternative pairing that doesn't happen to open a seat for an untested player.

Notice what your risk argument actually supports. If evil laid low for two missions, their best move right now is precisely what you are advocating: reject a tested pair, burn rejection slots toward five, or force an untested player onto the decisive mission. You have given the table no reason to believe Kenji or Theo specifically is that player — only that someone might be, which is equally true of any roster you would propose. I led Mission 2 and played Success. By your own logic, I know that the pool of candidates alongside me is exactly Kenji and Theo. I do not treat two successes as clearances, and I have said so myself. But they are the only public data we have, and both point away from the players campaigning hardest against this team and toward the players who keep positioning themselves for a seat or a rejection.

Leo, your earlier point that two successes don't clear Kenji or Theo is mechanically true, and I've acknowledged it. But it cuts equally against your own demand: you have never been on a team, never generated any mission data, and your entire argument remains private self-knowledge, which every player at this table shares equally.

Elena, direct question, and I'd like a direct answer: name one concrete, public piece of evidence against Kenji or Theo specifically — not a hypothetical about what evil might have done, but something either of them actually said or did. If you cannot, say plainly whether you will approve this team or keep pushing for a rejection that only helps whoever wants this mission to fail.

Felix, to answer your question directly: you are asking for concrete historical proof of malice in a game where evil has every incentive to lay low until match point. The lack of a fail card on Mission 1 or 2 is not proof of Theo's or Kenji's loyalty—it is simply proof that evil did not choose to reveal itself prematurely. 

What is concrete and right in front of us is Kenji's immediate decision to cut you out the moment you led Mission 2 to success. You took full accountability on Mission 2, put yourself on the roster, and the team succeeded. Now, on the single mission that decides whether Good wins or Evil steals the game, Kenji has discarded you entirely to lock down a private, two-person room with Theo. 

From your perspective, you know your own card was Success, but you cannot have absolute certainty about both Kenji and Theo. If either of them has bided their time, you are handing them the entire game while leaving yourself completely powerless to affect the outcome. I will not vote to approve this team because rubber-stamping a pairing that deliberately excludes the one player who just demonstrated leadership is an unnecessary risk. 

Felix, if you know you are Good and delivered Mission 2, why are you so eager to give up all personal agency on match point instead of questioning why Kenji dropped you?

Elena asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: yes, I'm comfortable letting Kenji and Theo decide match point, and I'm not troubled by being left off the roster. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
